Suffrage
sŭf´frĕj
n. (a vote or voice given in a choice; the congregation's part in choosing its officers)
Latin suffragium, a vote. The Reformed churches recovered the congregation's suffrage against the practice of appointment from above, on the ground that the New Testament churches had it.

Biblical Definition

Suffrage is the voice the people have in a choice. The New Testament churches had one. When deacons were needed, the apostles told the congregation to look out seven men, “and the saying pleased the whole multitude: and they chose Stephen” (Act 6:5). Matthias was set forth by the assembly before the lot was cast (Act 1:23–26). Elders were ordained “in every church” with the congregation present (Act 14:23). A brother was “chosen of the churches to travel with us” with the offering (2Co 8:19). And the Jerusalem decree was issued when “it pleased the apostles and elders, with the whole church” (Act 15:22).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines suffrage as a vote; a voice given in deciding a controverted question, or in the choice of a man for an office or trust; and united voice in competition, testimony in favor.

expand to see more

SUFFRAGE, n. A vote; a voice given in deciding a controverted question, or in the choice of a man for an office or trust.

Nothing can be more grateful to a good man than to be elevated to office by the unbiased suffrages of free enlightened citizens.

2. United voice of persons in public prayer.

3. Aid; assistance. [Not in use.]

Key Scripture

Act 6:5 — "And the saying pleased the whole multitude: and they chose Stephen, a man full of faith and of the Holy Ghost, and Philip, and Prochorus, and Nicanor, and Timon, and Parmenas, and Nicolas a proselyte of Antioch:"

Act 1:23 — "And they appointed two, Joseph called Barsabas, who was surnamed Justus, and Matthias."

Act 14:23 — "And when they had ordained them elders in every church, and had prayed with fasting, they commended them to the Lord, on whom they believed."

2Co 8:19 — "And not that only, but who was also chosen of the churches to travel with us with this grace, which is administered by us to the glory of the same Lord, and declaration of your ready mind:"

Act 15:22 — "Then pleased it the apostles and elders, with the whole church, to send chosen men of their own company to Antioch with Paul and Barnabas; namely, Judas surnamed Barsabas, and Silas, chief men among the brethren:"

Modern Corruption

A congregation's voice is either abolished or absolutised, and Acts shows it exercised inside apostolic direction.

expand to see more

Acts 6 is the model and its balance is easy to miss because both halves are in the same sentence. The apostles set the criteria — men of honest report, full of the Holy Ghost and wisdom — and the number, and they define the task. The congregation does the choosing. Then the apostles appoint the men the congregation chose. Neither party acts alone, and neither is a formality. That is what the Reformed have meant by the people's suffrage: a real voice, exercised within a real teaching authority, on candidates measured by a standard neither side invented.

Abolish the congregation's part and you get appointment from above, which is what the Reformation found and objected to — men set over churches that had never seen them, with the flock's only options being submission or departure. Absolutise it and you get a congregation that treats the pastorate as an employment decision and its own preferences as the qualification, which is the modern form of the same disease. Second Corinthians 8:19 is a useful check on both: the brother was chosen of the churches, and the purpose was that the handling of a large sum should be visibly above suspicion.

Acts 15:22 is worth noting for what it establishes about the most consequential decision the early church made. The apostles and elders deliberated; the conclusion was theirs; and it pleased them with the whole church to send chosen men to Antioch with the letter. The congregation was not polled on the doctrine of justification, and it was not bypassed either. A church order that cannot reproduce that sentence — with a real eldership and a real church, both in it — has lost something Luke thought worth recording.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek eklegomai (G1586), to choose out; cheirotoneo (G5500), to appoint, originally by show of hands; aresko (G700), to please; plethos (G4128), the multitude, the whole body.

expand to see more

Greek cheirotoneo (G5500) — to appoint; from cheir, hand — Acts 14:23, 2 Corinthians 8:19.

Greek exelexanto (G1586) — they chose; Acts 6:5, 15:22, 15:25.

Greek plethos (G4128) — the whole multitude; Acts 6:2, 6:5, 15:12, 15:30.

Usage

"“The saying pleased the whole multitude: and they chose” — a real voice."

"“Chosen of the churches to travel with us” — and the money was the reason."

"“The apostles and elders, with the whole church” — both, in one clause."
